newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Concern over weak dlr, supply.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Concern over weak dlr, supply.

text.p: If U.S. Treasury market participants wanted to find solace in the tedious and wearisome pace of activity thus far this week, they need only keep in mind that Thursday's retail sales report is just one day away.
In the meantime, players said, Wednesday should look similar to trading the first two days of the week: no data, low volume and influences from outside the Treasury market.
Wednesday is "going to be a day of where guys want to be going into retail sales," said a trader at a large U.S. bank.

Most players are said to be positioned where they want to be for the May retail sales report, in which economists expect a 0.4 percent rise for overall retail sales and a 0.3 percent increase for sales excluding autos.

Therefore, most anticipate another dull, low volume session. However, they put an asterik next to that theory, because of numerous outside factors -- mainly negative -- that could pressure the market.
First and foremost, the hedge fund selling that was seen on Tuesday could continue into Wednesday.
Cary Leahey, money market economist at Lehman Brothers, said that the selling, which came at session highs, may be the start of the market repricing itself.
"Perhaps the market went too far in the aftermath of employment," he said, referring to the big rally despite a perceived strong tone to the May jobs data on Friday.
"The Fed's not out of the ballgame," Leahey said. "The market has to reprice that."
In that case, the market would have to eventually back up to the 6.25 percent level on the two-year note seen before the Fed's May meeting.

Late Tuesday, the two-year note stood at around 6.13 percent, deemed too rich in light of current economic fundamentals of a tight labor market and fairly strong growth. That's why market participants see more risk to the downside than to the upside, even with positive technical factors.
Also, a deteriorating dollar weighed on the market on Monday and Tuesday, and players said the dollar's volatility could be a factor on Wednesday as well.
The dollar, which had been at 116 yen late last week, fell to 112 yen in the early part of this week. The dollar was down to 1.7170 marks from a 39-month high of 1.7425 on Friday.
Further problems for the market come in the form of supply, mainly corporate and mortgage backeds, traders said.
"There are probably a half-dozen deals out there," said a trader, adding that corporate and mortgage issues are highly attractive.
In late afternoon trading on Tuesday, the 30-year bond was at 97-10/32, down 5/32, to yield 6.84 percent.
Fed funds are seen opening around their 5-1/2 percent target rate on Wednesday. Some analysts said the Fed may make an outright purchase of either bills or coupons as early as Wednesday.
